title: Enkidu: From the Herd to Erech
subtitle: Food, clothing, and a new social role

learningObjectives.text: What does the Pennsylvania Tablet say Enkidu had not learned before?
What role does Enkidu take among the shepherds in this passage?

change.work: An Old Babylonian Version of the Gilgamesh Epic
change.author: Anonymous
change.translator: Morris Jastrow and Albert T. Clay
change.locator: Pennsylvania Tablet · Column III · part 1; Pennsylvania Tablet · Column III · part 1, normalized characters 115-785
change.excerpt: Enkidu had not known To eat food. To drink wine He had not been taught. The woman opened her mouth and Spoke to Enkidu: "Eat food, O Enkidu, The provender of life! Drink wine, the custom of the land!" Enkidu ate food Till he was satiated. Wine he drank, Seven goblets. His spirit was loosened, he became hilarious. His heart became glad and His face shone. [The barber(?)] removed The hair on his body. He was anointed with oil. He became manlike. He put on a garment, He was like a man. He took his weapon; Lions he attacked, (so that) the night shepherds could rest. He plunged the dagger; Lions he overcame. The great [shepherds] lay down; Enkidu was their protector.
change.note: Verbatim translation from the named Old Babylonian tablet witness in this edited edition. Brackets and question marks signal textual restoration or uncertainty.

narrativeBlocks.title: A new kind of meal
narrativeBlocks.body: The Pennsylvania Tablet describes Enkidu learning to eat prepared food and drink wine with the woman who leads him away from the herds.

narrativeBlocks.title: Learning the customs of the land
narrativeBlocks.body: Source quotation (Jastrow and Clay's tablet translation; whitespace normalized): “Enkidu had not known To eat food. To drink wine He had not been taught. The woman opened her mouth and Spoke to Enkidu: "Eat food, O Enkidu, The provender of life! Drink wine, the custom of the land!" Enkidu ate food Till he was satiated. Wine he drank, Seven goblets. His spirit was loosened, he became hilarious. His heart became glad and His face shone. [The barber(?)] removed The hair on his body. He was anointed with oil. He became manlike. He put on a garment, He was like a man. He took his weapon; Lions he attacked, (so that) the night shepherds could rest. He plunged the dagger; Lions he overcame. The great [shepherds] lay down; Enkidu was their protector.”

narrativeBlocks.title: A changed role
narrativeBlocks.body: The passage says Enkidu is anointed, clothed, and becomes a protector of shepherds against lions. It presents a shift in social role, not a timeless claim about 'civilization.'

narrativeBlocks.title: Notice uncertain words
narrativeBlocks.body: This is Jastrow and Clay's translation of a damaged tablet. Even its phrase '[The barber(?)]' is uncertain; do not convert the translator's reconstruction into a secure detail.

narrativeBlocks.title: Transformation through relationships
narrativeBlocks.body: Enkidu's change is narrated through food, clothing, speech, and his work among shepherds.
